ENT Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 2–3-day history of wheeze and shortness of breath; possible triggers discussed include viral infection and seasonal pollen; no specific food, drug, or environmental exposure identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Onset 2–3 days ago; worsening exertional dyspnea to the point patient can no longer walk to work; occasional difficulty completing sentences; no nocturnal symptoms; feels “well” at rest today.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: Denied.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: Denied.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: Denied.  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: None reported despite history of hay fever.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing: Wheeze only; no stridor.  
  • Dyspnea: Present on exertion; absent at rest.  
  • Swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): None.  
  • Ear/neck symptoms: None.
- Relevant past episodes/treatments: Childhood asthma with intermittent hospital visits; uses salbutamol inhaler “every few weeks” and before exercise; last regular asthma therapy discontinued 3–4 years ago.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Drug/food allergies: None reported.  
  • Medications: Salbutamol inhaler PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented in detail); no other regular meds; no antihistamine currently.
- Social: 33-year-old engineer; lives with partner; non-smoker; drinks ~1 glass wine every 2–3 days; currently working from home/sick leave.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: Not observed (video consultation).
- Airway/breathing: Patient reports wheeze on exertion; speaking full sentences during call; no visible distress reported.
- Mental status/associated features: Alert; denies dizziness or syncope.
- Vitals/exam: Temperature self-checked 37 °C; all other vitals “Not recorded.”
- Accompanied: Lives with partner; partner not present on call.

Assessment:
Working impression: Acute asthma exacerbation, likely provoked by viral upper-respiratory infection and/or seasonal allergen exposure.
Evidence summary: History of asthma, atopy (hay fever/eczema), abrupt 2–3-day worsening with wheeze and exertional dyspnea; normal temperature and absence of infectious sputum or chest pain support asthma flare over pneumonia/PE.
DDx (consistent with transcript):
1. Acute asthma exacerbation – most likely; classic symptoms and past history.
2. Viral respiratory tract infection/acute bronchitis – possible co-trigger; mild self-reported “fever” and cough.
3. Allergic (pollen-induced) asthma flare – atopic background; no current rhinitis symptoms noted (opposing evidence).

Plan:
- Medications/Devices:
  • Salbutamol: Increase to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours PRN via spacer.  
  • Spacer and peak-flow meter prescribed; pharmacist to demonstrate use.  
  • OTC antihistamine recommended daily for hay-fever control.
- Monitoring:
  • Record peak-flow values morning and evening for 1 week.  
  • Track symptom frequency and inhaler use.
- Escalation criteria/red flags: Seek immediate medical care (999/EMS) if resting dyspnea, inability to speak full sentences, chest tightness unrelieved by inhaler, stridor, lip/tongue/throat swelling, dizziness/syncope, or temperature rises.
- Follow-up:
  • Remote asthma review in 1 week with recorded peak-flow data.  
  • Consider step-up therapy (e.g., inhaled corticosteroid) at review if control remains poor.  
  • Reinforce inhaler technique and adherence.
- Education: Importance of regular reliever use during flare, avoidance of known triggers, keeping partner informed.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing expected elements: Full vital signs (HR, RR, BP, O2 sat), objective lung/ENT exam, detailed salbutamol dosing regimen, current availability of emergency reliever at workplace, formal asthma action plan, documentation of vaccination status (e.g., COVID-19, flu).  
● Transcript–DDx conflicts: None significant noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional repetitions but clinically adequate.
